activities.anchor: Two classical results price the trade-off
activities.caption: pair each inventory tool with its rule
activities.name: opsInventoryMatch

config.prompt: The warehouse's toolkit — pair each tool with what it does:

pairs.right: balances ordering cost against holding cost — optimum grows with √demand, not demand
order more as the margin of a sale rises and the cost of leftover falls
expected demand during the supplier's lead time plus safety stock
most of the buffer is organisational scar tissue you could remove by fixing the process

config.why: Inventory is simultaneously a service and a cost — conventionally 20–30 per cent of the item's value per year to hold.

activities.anchor: The counter-movement has its own name and its own decade
activities.caption: run the resilience decision
activities.name: opsShockBranch

config.root: A grounded ship has halted roughly a tenth of world trade. Your just-in-time line idles over components worth a few dollars. Now what?

start.text: The board asks what changes. Your first move?

choices.label: Add buffer stock of critical components
choices.feedback: Resilience is insurance with a premium: real money in good times, catastrophic payoff in bad ones.

choices.label: Dual-source the vulnerable components
choices.feedback: Two suppliers for one part — redundancy bought at margin cost.

choices.label: Stay pure JIT — the shock will pass
choices.feedback: The 2021 Suez blockage and the semiconductor shortages are what pure JIT bought: idled factories over dollar-parts.

buffer.text: Next question: engineering support — outsource it or run it yourself?

choices.label: Outsource — the unit price is lower
choices.feedback: Unit price is the lazy answer: hidden coordination costs are why 'simple' outsourcing projects overrun.

choices.label: Keep it in-house
choices.feedback: Capability stays: firms that outsourced engineering sometimes found they had outsourced their future.

dual.text: Redundancy in place — regional suppliers and visible pipelines are next on the same logic.

pure.text: The premium goes unpaid — and the next shock collects it with interest.

outsource.text: Cheaper per unit, costlier per surprise — price the dependency before signing.

inhouse.text: Control and capability retained — the premium runs through the payroll.

config.why: Which premium is worth paying is now a board-level question, not an operations footnote.

activities.caption: one line of the lean summary is wrong
activities.name: opsLeanSpot

config.prompt: One line of this lean/JIT summary is wrong. Find it.
lines: Lean means producing exactly what is needed, when needed, with zero waste
Waste includes overproduction, waiting, transport, excess inventory, motion, defects and unused talent
Just-in-time arranges for components to arrive as they are used
JIT works because extra inventory hides defects until they are cheap to fix
The philosophy rests on quality being high enough that zero buffer is survivable
config.correction: JIT works because inventory approaches zero and defects surface immediately instead of hiding in a warehouse.
config.why: The entire philosophy rests on quality being high enough that zero buffer is survivable — hiding defects is what the buffer used to do.

activities.anchor: Work it: fixed costs 10,000 a month
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the break-even run
activities.name: opsBreakevenCloze

config.text: Fixed costs 10,000 a month, price 25, variable cost 15 — contribution %%0%% per unit. Sell 900 and the month loses %%1%%; sell 1,300 and profit is %%2%%.
config.hint: Each unit past break-even drops its whole contribution to the bottom line.

config.prompt: A system's average queue length as utilisation approaches capacity — which curve is it?

curves.label: B: rises in a straight line

config.why: Waiting times explode non-linearly: a system at 90 per cent busy has roughly double the queue of one at 80 — and near-infinite queues at 99. Idle capacity in the right place is a service, not a waste.

activities.anchor: rises roughly tenfold at each stage it travels
activities.caption: call the multiplier — the 1–10–100 rule
activities.name: opsDefectEstimate

config.prompt: A defect caught at design costs 1. Roughly how many times more does the same defect cost once caught at production?
config.why: The 1–10–100 rule: design 1, production 10, the customer's hands 100 — recall campaigns, reputational damage, litigation.
config.context: Quality is usually the cost-cutter: rework, scrap, returns and lost customers are quietly among the largest lines in any operation's cost base.

activities.anchor: Unit-cost comparisons routinely omit coordination costs
activities.caption: true or false — the location ledger
activities.name: opsLocationJudge

statements.s: The cheapest location is the best location.
statements.why: The comparison omits coordination costs, quality variance, lead times, currency risk and the political risk of depending on one geography.

statements.s: Longer lead times inflate the inventory you must carry.
statements.why: Lead time is where the reorder point and safety stock come from.

statements.s: The firms that repatriated production after 2020 were discovering sentiment, not missing line items.
statements.why: They were discovering the missing line items.

statements.s: Location has quietly become a risk-management question as much as a cost question.
statements.why: Nearshoring, friend-shoring and reshoring all price fragility, tariffs and logistics shocks.
